subtopic: Radicalising rage online
passage:
At the tea stall by the bus stop in their village, Shankar showed his cousin Lokesh a video on his phone. 'Look. They're saying the dam money was stolen by outsiders. It makes my blood boil.'
Lokesh, who taught at the block school, didn't argue about the dam. He asked, 'Who made it? Why does the music get louder there? Why does it end with "share before they delete it"?'
Shankar watched it again. It was true: the music swelled, the words came in red, the ending told him to share, not to check.
That weekend Lokesh showed him how the app picks what to show: the more you react, the more it sends. Shankar muted four angry channels. He followed the district newspaper and a farmers' radio show that interviewed people on different sides.
Next time a red-lettered video came up, he felt the heat rise and stopped. Built to make me angry, he thought. He scrolled past.

qa.q: What did the video say about the dam money?
qa.a: It said the dam money was stolen by outsiders.

qa.q: What was Shankar thinking when he stopped at the next red-lettered video?
qa.a: He recognised that the video was built to make him angry, and chose not to react.

qa.q: Which steps helped Shankar break the anger loop?
qa.a: Learning how feeds reward reactions, muting angry channels, following sources with more than one side, and pausing before reacting.

qa.q: How might Lokesh feel seeing his cousin scroll past such videos now?
qa.a: Lokesh may feel relieved and proud, having helped by asking questions rather than lecturing.

grounding: It shows a teen learning how feeds are built to provoke, muting rage channels, following varied sources and noticing anger-bait before reacting.

subtopic: Radicalising rage online
passage:
In the Izmir school library, the media studies teacher, Ms Kaya, put a post on the screen: a photo of a crowded bus with the caption 'THEY are taking over YOUR city. Share if you're angry!'
'Before you react,' Ms Kaya said, 'find three tricks.'
Zeynep, sixteen, felt her pulse tick up, and then made herself look. Capital letters. 'They' with no name. An order to share, no link to a source. Pablo, next to her, spotted a fourth: the photo was from another country, five years old.
That evening Zeynep went through her own feed. The more she'd clicked on angry posts, she realised, the more it had shown her. She muted six accounts that only ever posted outrage and followed two news sites that showed different sides of the same story.
On Friday a furious video popped up. Zeynep caught herself mid-thumb. Built to make me mad, she thought, and checked the source first.

qa.q: Where was the photo of the crowded bus actually from?
qa.a: The photo was from another country, five years old.

qa.q: How did Zeynep feel when she first saw the post, and what did she do with that feeling?
qa.a: She felt her pulse tick up with anger, then made herself slow down and look for the tricks.

qa.q: What skill did Zeynep build, and why is it useful?
qa.a: She learned to notice when a post is designed to anger before reacting, and to mute rage accounts and follow varied sources, so her feed stops steering her feelings.

qa.q: How might Pablo's discovery about the photo change how their classmates see such posts?
qa.a: It may make them more careful, realising how easily an old photo can be used to make them angry.

grounding: It shows a teen learning how posts and feeds are built to provoke, muting rage accounts, following varied sources and checking before reacting.
